extracted.intended_audience: Department of Energy guidance authors; regulatory analysts, OMB/OIRA staff, and policymakers involved in regulatory impact and equity analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for incorporating equity and distributional considerations into regulatory impact analysis, including which metrics and methods agencies should use to measure and weigh distributional impacts (with a focused application to clean hydrogen emissions accounting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed OMB guidance on conducting granular distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide detailed guidance to agencies on conducting granular analysis, assessing costs and benefits for a manageable number of demographic subgroups, and weighing distributional concerns alongside other regulatory impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should include how to conduct subgroup-level analysis, which subgroups to consider (a manageable set), how to present distributional results alongside aggregate effects, and mechanisms for OMB and the Domestic Policy Council (DPC) to facilitate interagency coordination to promote equity across the regulatory system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use marginal emissions rates with spatial and temporal granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: For calculating carbon intensity of hydrogen produced with grid electricity, DOE's final guidance should endorse the use of marginal emissions rates with appropriate spatial and temporal granularity rather than annual-average grid factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marginal emissions rates with proper spatial/temporal resolution better reflect the true emissions consequences of using grid electricity, and they incentivize clean hydrogen production when and where renewable generation would otherwise be curtailed. Relying on annual-average approaches (such as GREET defaults) can significantly miscalculate facility-level emissions and undermine CHPS goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use models/data appropriate to the decision context (GREET vs. facility assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The default emissions assumptions of GREET may be reasonable for selecting an overall CHPS target, but assessing the performance of a given facility requires different, higher-granularity data (e.g., marginal rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the same annual-average/default model inputs for both setting broad program-level targets and for facility- or project-level compliance/accounting. Specify which models/approaches are appropriate for which purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify distribution of costs and benefits and assess unquantified outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should quantify the distribution of costs and benefits and provide detailed information on the nature, timing, likelihood, location, and distribution of unquantified benefits and costs (as encouraged by Circular A-4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should report disaggregated monetary and non-monetary effects across relevant subgroups and geographies and explicitly characterize uncertainties and unquantified outcomes, per Circular A-4 and EPA guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ inequality metrics to characterize distributional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inequality measures (e.g., Gini coefficient, Atkinson Index, Theil Index, segregation measures) to characterize the degree of inequality across social groups in defined health outcomes and how that inequality changes under regulatory alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different metrics provide different policy-relevant information; analysts should choose metrics appropriate to the policymaker's questions and may present multiple metrics to illustrate complementary aspects of distributional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric selection should satisfy specific axioms (Pigou-Dalton, decomposability, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to cited best-practice axioms, a chosen inequality indicator should: avoid implicit value judgments about relative importance of percentile transfers; incorporate differential susceptibility (e.g., health risk differences); include baseline distributions of risk; use appropriate geographic resolution and scope; consider multiple competing policy alternatives; satisfy the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle; and be subgroup-decomposable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending or using a metric, document how the metric meets these desiderata and why it is appropriate for the analysis' objectives and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate benefit estimates across demographic groups (avoid uniform application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts should disaggregate health and benefit estimates across demographic groups rather than applying uniform (aggregate) benefit estimates (e.g., a single dollar value of statistical life) across all groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregation captures differences in baseline risk and differential susceptibility; it reduces the risk that uniform valuation obscures distributional impacts or produces perverse redistributions (e.g., directing resources to wealthier communities because of higher asset values). Cite guidance favoring disaggregation (e.g., UK guidance, EPA technical guidance, and health-impact quantification how-to guides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social welfare functions and distributional/priority weights, with institutional/legal caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may use social welfare functions or distributional/prioritarian weights to factor equity into benefit-cost analysis, recognizing these approaches formalize preferences for improving well-being of the worse-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While theoretically justifiable, the use of distributional weights raises interpersonal-comparison, moral-preference, and institutional-legitimacy concerns (who sets weights?). Agencies should document the rationale for weights, consider legal constraints, and anticipate judicial scrutiny; weight design may consider income, health status, longevity, or other attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fine-scale/local data to maximize health benefits and minimize inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate local-scale data in the design and evaluation of air quality and other environmental policies to identify location-specific mitigation opportunities and reduce inequality in health outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-resolution data can reveal heterogeneous damages and local mitigation opportunities that coarser averages miss; using such data helps avoid allocating resources in ways that favor wealthier areas due to higher asset valuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize legal constraints when incorporating protected characteristics (e.g., race) into analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Using race or other suspect classifications as explicit factors in decisionmaking or in mathematical weighting schemes may raise constitutional and legal issues; courts have been skeptical of mechanistic analyses that treat race as a quantitative 'point allocation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering race or similarly sensitive attributes, agencies should assess legal risk, document statutory authority and tailoring, and consider alternative, race-neutral proxies or targeted, legitimate programmatic justifications; expect judicial scrutiny where explicit racial weighting is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate methodological choices across agencies because of cross-rulemaking effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological choices made by one agency (e.g., DOE's emissions accounting for CHPS) can influence other agencies' rulemakings or program implementations (e.g., Treasury's clean-hydrogen tax credit rules); agencies should consider these cross-agency implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should document potential downstream impacts of methodological choices and, where appropriate, coordinate with other agencies to ensure consistent and legally defensible approaches across related programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure distributional analyses are meaningful and defensible to avoid judicial reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should conduct meaningful evaluation of distributional impacts because courts have rebuked agencies for perfunctory or inadequate distributional analyses (e.g., USDA SNAP ABAWD rule found arbitrary and capricious for failing to meaningfully evaluate distributional impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent methods, data, subgroup selection rationale, sensitivity analyses, and clear explanation of how distributional findings informed the agency's decision to reduce exposure to arbitrary-and-capricious litigation risk.
